p172.002: On Friday afternoon, March 31, A.D. 30, Jesus and the apostles arrived at Bethany. So many people were coming because they had heard of Lazarus's resurrection that Jesus stayed at the home of Simon, a neighboring believer. Many people expected Jesus to ignore the Sanhedrin's death sentence, enter Jerusalem, and become king of the Jews, but Lazarus, Martha, and Mary knew that Jesus was not that kind of king, and they sensed that this might be his last visit. The chief priests were afraid to seize Jesus while he was among his friends, so they waited for him to come into Jerusalem. Jesus knew all of this, yet he was calmer and gentler than ever.
p172.004: On the evening after the Sabbath ended, the people of Bethany and Bethpage held a banquet at Simon's house for Jesus and Lazarus. Jesus talked about Joshua of old and said, “⟦Q 172:1.3⟧I would cause the walls of prejudice, self-righteousness, and hate to crumble⟦/Q⟧”. As the banquet was ending, Mary opened a jar of very costly ointment, poured it on Jesus' head and feet, and wiped them with her hair. The whole house was filled with the fragrance. When some people began to murmur, Judas Iscariot complained to Andrew that it should have been sold to help the poor.
p172.005: Jesus laid his hand on Mary's head and said that the poor could be helped at any time, but that he was soon going to the Father, and that Mary, believing his words about his death, had kept this ointment for his burial. He also said that wherever the gospel was preached, what she had done would be told. The Urantia Book says that Judas took this rebuke as a reproach aimed at himself, and that for the first time he clearly began to think of revenge. When the chief priests heard about this, they decided that Lazarus must be killed too.
p172.007: On Sunday morning, in Simon's garden, Jesus gave the twelve apostles their last instructions. During this Passover they were not to teach or preach in public, but to stay near him and to “⟦Q 172:2.1⟧watch and pray.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus knew that some of the apostles were hiding swords, but he said nothing about it. Then he briefly looked back over their ministry, from the day they were ordained as apostles at Capernaum until now. He also urged Lazarus not to lose his life at the hands of the Sanhedrin. The people vaguely sensed that a crisis was coming, but Jesus was so unusually cheerful and full of humor that they did not realize how serious it was.
p172.009: Jesus loved Bethany dearly. Nazareth, Capernaum, and Jerusalem had rejected him, but Bethany believed in him. Until now Jesus had always stopped people from hailing him as the Messiah, but this time was different. Since his death sentence had already been decided, there was no harm in letting his disciples express their joy freely. Jesus was not seeking popularity or power, and he knew exactly how this visit would end.
p172.010: Jesus decided to ride in humbly on a donkey's colt, as in the prophecy of Zechariah. A king coming to make war rode a horse, but a king bringing peace rode a donkey. He meant to show by action what he had not been able to make them understand by words: that his kingdom was a spiritual kingdom of peace. The people spread their cloaks and branches on the road and shouted, “⟦Q 172:3.9⟧Hosanna to the son of David⟦/Q⟧”. In Jerusalem, too, thousands who had heard the news came out to meet him, waving palm branches.
p172.011: But at the top of the Mount of Olives, when the city and the temple came into view, Jesus stopped the procession and wept. He grieved that Jerusalem did not know the things that would bring her peace and was about to reject the Son of Peace, and that someday her enemies would surround the city and not leave one stone upon another. When the Pharisees told him to quiet his disciples, Jesus answered that if they were silenced, “⟦Q 172:3.13⟧these stones by the roadside cry out.⟦/Q⟧” The Urantia Book says that this joyful welcome was glad and sincere but not deep faith, and that a few days later, when the same crowd was disappointed, they quickly abandoned Jesus.
p172.013: The Sanhedrin was afraid of the people and did not dare touch Jesus. The Urantia Book explains that this public entry was the only human way to keep him from being arrested as soon as he entered the city. Jesus wanted to give the people of Jerusalem and the tens of thousands of pilgrims one last chance to hear the gospel. In the evening, when the crowds had gone, Jesus and the apostles sat by the temple treasury and watched people give their offerings. The rich put in a great deal, but a poor widow put in two small copper coins. Jesus said, “⟦Q 172:4.2⟧This poor widow cast in more than all the others⟦/Q⟧”, because she had given all that she had.
p172.015: On the way back to Bethany, no one spoke. Each apostle was caught up in different feelings. Andrew was busy watching to make sure his excited companions did not do something rash. Peter was deeply sad that he had not been able to preach the gospel to the gathered crowds, and James was disappointed that a good chance to proclaim the kingdom had been missed. John, remembering Zechariah's prophecy, partly understood the symbolic meaning of the king of peace. Philip was relieved that he had not been asked to feed the crowd, but doubts about the kingdom came to him, and Nathaniel and Thomas realized that the procession was meant to keep the Sanhedrin from arresting Jesus at once. Matthew was deeply discouraged, but by morning he had regained his spirits.
p172.016: Simon Zelotes, dreaming of Jesus taking David's throne, shouted the loudest, but by the afternoon he had fallen into deep disappointment. For the Alpheus twins, on the other hand, this was a perfect day, the closest thing to heaven, and the memory of it held them up until the hour of the cross. The one most badly affected was Judas. To him Jesus, riding on a donkey, looked more like a clown than a king, and when a Sadducean friend mocked him at the city gate, he grew ashamed of his Master and his companions. The Urantia Book says that in his heart he had already become a deserter. That people can see the same event and take it so differently, depending on the state of their hearts, reminds us how important it is what we keep our eyes on as we live.
p173.002: Early Monday morning, Jesus and the apostles gathered at Simon's house in Bethany and then set out for Jerusalem. The apostles were silent, their minds full of the events of the day before. All of them were thinking, “⟦Q 173:0.2⟧What will the Master do today?⟦/Q⟧” Only Judas was struggling with a different question: “⟦Q 173:0.2⟧What shall I do? Shall I go on with Jesus and my associates, or shall I withdraw?⟦/Q⟧” Arriving at the temple about nine o'clock in the morning, Jesus went up onto the platform in the great court where he usually taught and began to speak to the people who gathered.
p173.004: By that time the temple had become a huge marketplace. Animals offered as sacrifices had to be free from all “⟦Q 173:1.1⟧blemish⟦/Q⟧”, and because the inspectors often rejected the animals people brought, people bought animals at the temple at high prices. Sometimes a poor person was charged as much as a week's wages for a pair of doves. Also, the temple tax could be paid only in Jewish silver coins, so the money-changers made large fees exchanging the pilgrims' money. The profits flowed to the high-priestly families, while the common people carried heavy burdens in poverty.
p173.005: Just as Jesus was about to teach, a quarrel broke out on one side, because a money-changer had cheated a Jew from Alexandria, and a herd of about a hundred bellowing cattle was driven past. On top of that, Jesus saw a simple Galilean being mocked by arrogant men. Jesus stepped down from the platform, took a whip of cords from a boy, drove the animals out of the temple, and opened the gates of all the pens. The excited pilgrims overturned the money-changers' tables, and in less than five minutes all the trading in the temple was gone. Jesus said that “⟦Q 173:1.7⟧My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations⟦/Q⟧”, but that they had made it a den of robbers.
p173.006: The people cheered and shouted hosanna, and that day the temple court was quiet and peaceful. The chief priests became even more afraid of Jesus, but they did not dare lay a hand on him because they feared the people. The Urantia Book says this event shows how much Jesus hated using religion to make money, and every injustice of exploiting the poor and the uneducated. It also shows that we should not let a small number of unjust people, backed by power, oppress the many.
p173.008: The Sanhedrin decided to get rid of Jesus quickly, but they could not agree on when or how. So they sent people to try to trap Jesus with words. About two o'clock in the afternoon, some elders came and asked, “⟦Q 173:2.2⟧By what authority do you do these things?⟦/Q⟧” In those days one could teach only with formal approval from the Sanhedrin, so this question was meant to paint Jesus as an unqualified teacher.
p173.009: Jesus asked them in return: was John's baptism from heaven or from men? They were stuck. If they said it was from heaven, he would ask why they had not believed John; if they said it was from men, the people, who held John to be a prophet, would be angry. In the end they answered, “⟦Q 173:2.5⟧we do not know⟦/Q⟧”, and Jesus said that he would not tell them about his authority either. The Urantia Book explains that this was not dodging the question. Jesus' authority came not from John or from the Sanhedrin but from the Father, and the people clearly saw the dishonesty of their leaders.
p173.011: Jesus told a parable. A father told his two sons to go and work in the vineyard. One son said, “⟦Q 173:3.1⟧I will not go⟦/Q⟧”, but later repented and went; the other said, “⟦Q 173:3.1⟧Yes, my father, I will go⟦/Q⟧”, but did not go. When Jesus asked who had done the father's will, the people answered, the first son. Jesus said that publicans and sinners, realizing their wrongs, would enter the kingdom of God before the religious leaders. Jesus did not hate people; he was rebuking the old religious system that was bound up in forms and traditions.
p173.013: Jesus told another parable. An owner planted a vineyard, rented it out to tenants, and went away to a far country. At harvest time he sent servants to collect the fruits, but the tenants beat the servants, stoned them, and even killed them. Last of all the owner sent his son, saying that “⟦Q 173:4.2⟧they will surely show respect for my beloved son⟦/Q⟧”, but the tenants killed the son too, to take the inheritance. The people answered that the owner would punish those wicked tenants and give the vineyard to others.
p173.014: Some, realizing that this parable spoke of the long history of rejecting the prophets and of how Jesus would soon be rejected, were saddened. Jesus pointed to the scripture about “⟦Q 173:4.4⟧the stone which the builders rejected⟦/Q⟧” becoming the cornerstone, and he warned that if they kept rejecting the gospel, the kingdom would be given to others who would bear fruit. The Pharisees knew he was speaking about them and were angry, but they were afraid of the crowd and could not seize Jesus. That night they joined hands with the Sadducees and planned to trap him the next day.
p173.016: Jesus also told the parable of the marriage feast. A king invited guests to his son's wedding feast, but they made excuses about their farms and their business and did not come, and some even harmed the messengers. The king sent people out to the roadsides and the out-of-the-way places, and invited everyone—good and bad, rich and poor—to fill the feast. But one man was not wearing the wedding garment the king had freely provided. The king sent him out, saying that he wanted only those who gladly accepted his invitation and wore the wedding garment to be there.
p173.017: When a believer asked for a sign by which they could know that Jesus was the Son of God, Jesus pointed to his own body and said, “⟦Q 173:5.4⟧Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.⟦/Q⟧” No one understood what he meant, but after the resurrection the apostles remembered these words. That evening, as the apostles went back to Bethany, they felt more strongly than ever that something tragic was coming, and they hardly slept. God invites everyone to the feast, but gladly answering that invitation is up to each of us.
p174.002: About seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, Jesus met with the apostles, the women's corps, and the leading disciples at Simon's house. Jesus said good-bye to Lazarus and told him to flee to Philadelphia, and he gave his last advice to the women's corps. Then he greeted each of the twelve apostles one by one. He told Andrew to keep a firm hold on his brothers, and Peter not to rely on the strength of the flesh or on swords but to stand on the eternal rocks. He told John to love even his enemies, and Thomas to walk by faith and not by sight. He told Simon Zelotes that even if he was crushed by disappointment, his spirit would rise again.
p174.003: To Judas he said, “⟦Q 174:0.2⟧Judas, I have loved you and have prayed that you would love your brethren⟦/Q⟧”, and he warned him to beware the slippery paths of flattery and the poison darts of ridicule. Then Jesus left for Jerusalem with Andrew, Peter, James, and John, while the other apostles went to set up the Gethsemane camp, which would be their headquarters from that day on. Partway down the Mount of Olives, Jesus stopped and talked with the four apostles for more than an hour.
p174.005: Peter and James disagreed about forgiveness. James said that the Father forgives us even before we ask, and Peter said that we are forgiven only after we first repent and confess. Jesus answered that neither of them truly understood the loving relationship between God and man. Wise and loving parents understand their children so deeply that they seldom drift far enough apart for forgiveness even to be needed.
p174.006: Because the Father in heaven understands and loves us infinitely, forgiveness is perfectly natural to God. When a child does wrong, the child feels separated from the father, but a true father never feels such a distance. “⟦Q 174:1.4⟧Sin is an experience of creature consciousness; it is not a part of God's consciousness.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said that when you understand another person's inner motives, you come to love him, and when you love him, you have already forgiven him. Being unable to forgive others is a sign that we have not yet grown up, and love begins with understanding, grows through service, and is made complete in wisdom.
p174.008: The night before, the Jewish leaders had decided to shame Jesus in front of the people before arresting him. Pharisees, Sadducees, and even Herodians joined together. On Tuesday morning, young students who had rehearsed beforehand came to Jesus, heaped false praise on him, pretending to be respectful, and then asked: Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, the Roman emperor? If he said not to pay, they could accuse him of treason against Rome; if he said to pay, the Jews, who were proud of their nation, would turn against him. That was their plan.
p174.009: Jesus had them bring a coin and asked whose image was on it. When they said Caesar's, Jesus said, “⟦Q 174:2.2⟧Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and render to God the things that are God's.⟦/Q⟧” Even the Sanhedrin had a rule at that time that whoever minted the coins had the right to collect taxes, so no one could find fault with this answer. Jesus was not dodging the question; he was simply dealing wisely with people who wanted to harm him.
p174.011: Next came the Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection, with a question. If seven brothers, one after another, had married the same woman and all had died without children, whose wife would she be in the resurrection? Jesus answered that they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those who are resurrected do not marry, and like the angels they become sons of God who never die again.
p174.012: Jesus answered with the words of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted. God had said, “⟦Q 174:3.2⟧I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.⟦/Q⟧” He did not say that he had been their God. God is not the God of the dead but of the living. The Urantia Book adds that although Jesus affirmed that people survive through the resurrection, he did not approve the Pharisees' belief that the same body comes back to life.
p174.014: Then a lawyer asked which commandment was the greatest. Jesus answered that to love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength is the first and greatest commandment, and that the second, which springs directly from the first, is “⟦Q 174:4.2⟧You shall love your neighbor as yourself.⟦/Q⟧” All the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments. The lawyer admitted that this love was more important than any sacrifice, and Jesus said, “⟦Q 174:4.3⟧I perceive that you are not far from the kingdom of God.⟦/Q⟧” In fact, that night he went to Jesus' camp, confessed his faith, and was baptized.
p174.015: After that no one dared to question him in public. Instead, Jesus asked them whose son the Messiah was. When they answered, the son of David, he asked how he could be David's son when David, in the Psalm, had called the Messiah “⟦Q 174:4.6⟧my lord⟦/Q⟧”. The leaders could not answer. The Pharisees and the Sadducees enjoyed each other's failures for a while, but to stop Jesus they soon forgot their old differences and joined hands. All the while, the common people listened to Jesus gladly.
p174.017: About noon, some Greek believers from Alexandria, Athens, and Rome asked Philip to let them meet Jesus. Philip, together with Andrew, took them to the house of Joseph. Jesus told the Jews and gentiles gathered there that the leaders of his own people had blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, but that he was glad to welcome these gentiles who had come seeking the light. And he said that whoever believes in him believes in the One who sent him, and “⟦Q 174:5.7⟧I am the light of the world⟦/Q⟧”. He had come not to judge the world but to save it.
p174.018: Jesus said that unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it cannot bear much fruit. And he said that his heart was troubled by what was coming, but that he would not pray to be saved from that hour; rather he would pray, “⟦Q 174:5.9⟧Father, glorify your name; your will be done.⟦/Q⟧” Then Jesus' Personalized Adjuster appeared and said that the Father's name would be glorified again. The people did not hear the voice, but they whispered that an angel had spoken to him.
p174.019: Jesus said that this had happened to encourage his disciples, and that when he was lifted up, he would draw all people into fellowship with the Father. After urging them to walk in the light while the light was with them, Jesus led the way back to the temple to say his last farewell to the leaders. Like Jesus, who prayed “⟦Q 174:5.9⟧your will be done⟦/Q⟧” even in a moment of fear, we too can learn the courage to trust God and leave things in his hands when times are hard.
p175.002: A little after two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, Jesus arrived in the temple court with the eleven apostles, Joseph of Arimathea, thirty Greeks, and some other disciples. Here Jesus began his last discourse. This discourse was his last appeal to the Jewish people and his last charge against the scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, and rulers of Israel who were seeking to destroy him. The money-changers and traders who had been driven out the day before did not dare to come back, so the court was quiet, and before beginning, Jesus looked over his audience with loving eyes.
p175.004: Jesus first said that he had long traveled through this land proclaiming the Father's love, and that many had entered the kingdom by faith. He and his apostles had always sought peace, but the leaders of Israel had rejected the light of God. Even so, Jesus said, “⟦Q 175:1.3⟧Even now it is not too late for this people to receive the word of heaven and to welcome the Son of Man.⟦/Q⟧” He held out one last chance to repent even to those who wanted to kill him. He warned that just as their fathers had killed the prophets, the present leaders were seeking to kill the Son of Man.
p175.005: Then Jesus told the people that since the scribes and Pharisees sat in the seat of Moses, they should go along with them in matters that kept the peace of the nation, but should not copy what they did. They said good things but did not do them; they loaded heavy burdens on people's shoulders but would not lift a finger; they craved high places and titles while secretly taking away the houses of widows. Jesus taught that spiritually, God alone is our Father, and that whoever wants to be greatest must serve everyone. And he made it clear that he held no ill will toward these leaders.
p175.006: Next Jesus rebuked their hypocrisy point by point with the words “⟦Q 175:1.12⟧Woe upon you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!⟦/Q⟧” He rebuked them for refusing to enter the kingdom themselves while keeping others out; for carefully tithing mint and dill while neglecting faith, mercy, and justice; for cleaning only the outside of the cup and leaving the inside dirty; and for being like whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside but full of bones inside. Yet to the very end Jesus offered mercy and forgiveness, and he grieved that he had wanted to gather them “⟦Q 175:1.23⟧as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings⟦/Q⟧”, but they would not. Finally he said that he would never again teach in the temple, and he left the temple with his followers.
p175.008: Here The Urantia Book adds an important warning. The fact that the leaders of the Jewish nation rejected Jesus and plotted his death in no way changes the standing of each individual Jew before God. Jesus himself was a Jew by birth, and the first martyrs who gave their lives for the gospel, such as Peter, Philip, and Matthew, were Jews. The Urantia Book says clearly that it was wrong for those who call themselves followers of Christ to hate and persecute the Jews for so many centuries, and that this story from history cannot justify such hatred.
p175.009: To torment children who bear no blame for the wrongs of their ancestors is cruel and irrational. To do so in the name of the one who taught us to love even our enemies is even worse. The Urantia Book stresses that the Father and the Creator Son have never stopped loving the Jews, that God does not judge people by outward appearance, and that salvation is offered to all.
p175.011: At eight o'clock that evening, the Sanhedrin, the highest court of the Jewish nation, met. There had been several decisions before to stop Jesus, but this time, just before midnight, they formally and unanimously voted to sentence Jesus and Lazarus to death. This decision, made even before any trial, was their answer to Jesus' last appeal for mercy. The Urantia Book explains that from this time on, the Jewish nation lost its special mission of bringing the light of truth to the world and remained a purely human nation.
p175.012: The officers of the Sanhedrin were ordered to arrest Jesus the next day, but out of the people's sight—if possible, by seizing him suddenly at night. And they were instructed to bring Jesus before the court before midnight on Thursday.
p175.014: After the discourse, the apostles were thrown into confusion again. Judas Iscariot had been discussing with his Sadducean relatives how to get out of the apostolic group, so he missed the merciful appeal in the first part of the discourse. Hearing the sharp rebukes in the last part, he made up his mind to abandon the gospel movement completely. Even so, he went with the apostles to the Mount of Olives and spent the night at the camp near Gethsemane. Meanwhile, at the home of Nicodemus, more than thirty Jewish leaders who secretly believed in Jesus promised to declare their loyalty openly the moment he was arrested, and they did.
p175.015: The Sadducees were afraid that the crowds following Jesus would lead to a clash with Rome; their income had dropped because of the cleansing of the temple; and they worried that the new teaching of the brotherhood of man would shake the social order. The Pharisees felt that Jesus had challenged their authority, ignored their Sabbath rules, and blasphemed by calling God his Father, and they were furious at the rebukes of that day. Some Sadducees proposed killing Jesus secretly, but the Pharisees would not agree. Vast numbers of heavenly beings wanted to help their sovereign, but they were held back and could only watch. To the very end, Jesus reached out even to those who wanted to harm him. Choosing mercy instead of hatred, as he did, is the love we must learn.
p176.002: On Tuesday afternoon, as they were leaving the temple, Matthew pointed to the huge stones and beautiful decorations and asked whether these buildings could really be destroyed. Jesus answered that soon “⟦Q 176:0.1⟧there shall not be left one stone upon another.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles believed that the temple could be destroyed only at the end of the world, so their curiosity grew. At sunset they climbed the Mount of Olives, looked down on the temple glowing in the evening light, and settled down under the full moon, and Nathaniel asked how they could know when this would happen.
p176.004: Jesus told them that after he left, many would appear claiming to be deliverers and would lead people astray, so they must be careful. They should not be alarmed by news of wars, famines, and earthquakes, and if they were persecuted and brought to court for the gospel, they should not worry about what to say, because the spirit would teach them what to say at that time. Jesus promised, “⟦Q 176:1.1⟧I will not forsake you; my spirit will not desert you⟦/Q⟧”, and he encouraged them that the gospel would in the end be proclaimed to all nations.
p176.005: Jesus knew that if the people rejected a spiritual Messiah and insisted on a worldly deliverer who would drive out Rome, they would eventually clash with the Roman armies and Jerusalem would be destroyed. So he told them that when they saw Roman armies surrounding Jerusalem, they should take nothing with them but flee at once to the mountains. In fact, the believers followed this warning, and when the Roman armies first appeared, they fled north to Pella and saved their lives.
p176.006: But many disciples tied this prophecy together with the Messiah coming again, setting up a new Jerusalem, and the world coming to an end. Peter, too, asked when the Master would come again. Jesus was sad that they kept misunderstanding because they always tried to attach new teachings to old ideas, but he explained it to them again.
p176.008: Jesus had said many times that he would leave the world but would someday return, and this became the belief in the second coming. Jesus said that his kingdom was not of this world, and that the present end would become a new beginning, in which the gospel would spread to the whole world. After he left, the Spirit of Truth, which would be poured out on all people, would comfort and guide them, and he promised that someday he would return, not in weakness and in the flesh, but in power and in the spirit. But he said that only the councils of Paradise know when that will be; not even the angels of heaven know.
p176.009: Jesus told them to read the signs of the times wisely, just as they know summer is near when the fig tree puts out leaves. He also applied the meaning of this teaching to individuals. When each person finishes this life and passes through the gate of death, he experiences personally what the whole world will go through at the end of an age. The Urantia Book explains that this night's teaching, which dealt with the two subjects of the destruction of Jerusalem and the second coming together, caused the greatest confusion, and that the gospel records were much distorted as other writings were mixed in. Only the apostle John did not become confused.
p176.011: In front of the campfire, Thomas asked what attitude they should live with while the Master was away. Jesus answered that their relationship with the kingdom is a spiritual and personal experience, formed by faith that they are sons of God. Even if nations fall, an age ends, and the world ends, the life of one who knows God and believes the gospel is eternally secure in the Father. Believers should keep the second coming in mind, but just as they live mindful of a death that may come at any time, they should faithfully do their work every day. Yet this faith is a living faith, and it must bear the fruits of the spirit more and more richly.
p176.012: Jesus told the parable of the talents. Before leaving on a journey, a master entrusted his servants with five talents, two talents, and one talent, each according to his ability. The first two servants worked hard and doubled what they had received, and they were praised: “⟦Q 176:3.4⟧Well done, good and faithful servant⟦/Q⟧”. But the servant who received one talent was afraid, buried it in the ground, gave it back just as it was, and blamed his master, and in the end even that was taken from him. Jesus said that in the work of the eternal kingdom one cannot stand still, and that service done to the least of his brethren is done to him.
p176.013: The Urantia Book says that truth is living. To lock truth into a rigid mold and say, “⟦Q 176:3.7⟧we have allowed no changes to be made in that which you taught us⟦/Q⟧”, is like the servant who buried his one talent. Whether we have received many gifts or few, what matters is whether we use them not only for ourselves but to serve others. That night Jesus ended the day with these words: “⟦Q 176:3.10⟧Freely have you received; therefore freely should you give of the truth of heaven⟦/Q⟧”.
p176.015: The Urantia Book says that of all the Master's teachings, the most misunderstood was his promise to come again. Michael, that is, Jesus, experienced his last bestowal as a mortal on this world, so it is only natural that he would want to come back here. Jesus made two promises. One was to send the Spirit of Truth, which was fulfilled at Pentecost. The other was to return personally someday, but he did not say when or how he would come. The early believers linked the second coming with the destruction of Jerusalem, and when that had passed and the Master still had not come, they came to link it with the end of the world.
p176.016: The beings who brought The Urantia Book say honestly that they believe Jesus will return, even more than once, but that they do not know when or how. So it is better not to tie the second coming to any particular event or date. In fact, through death a person goes straight on to the presence of Jesus, the sovereign of our universe, so there is no need to worry about whether he comes to us or we go to him. The Urantia Book urges, “⟦Q 176:4.7⟧Be you therefore ever ready to welcome him on earth⟦/Q⟧”. Rather than fearing the distant future, the best way to be ready is to faithfully use the gifts we have received today and to serve our neighbors.
p177.002: When they were not busy teaching, Jesus and the apostles rested every Wednesday. On this Wednesday morning, the camp was wrapped in a heavy silence. Jesus told the apostles to rest that day and think deeply about what had happened in Jerusalem and what was still to come, but he told them not to go inside the gates of Jerusalem. When David Zebedee, saying it was dangerous, offered to send three armed guards with him, Jesus said that no one could lay a hand on him until the time came to lay down his life according to the Father's will, and that he would go alone. Just then young John Mark came up carrying a basket of food and water.
p177.004: When Jesus reached for the basket, John Mark held on to it tightly and said that if he carried it and came along, the Master would be freer to pray. The two of them stood there, both holding the basket, until Jesus let go first and said, “⟦Q 177:1.2⟧Since with all your heart you crave to go with me, it shall not be denied you.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus spent his last quiet day on earth in the hills with this boy, talking with the Father. On high this day is called “⟦Q 177:1.3⟧the day which a young man spent with God in the hills.⟦/Q⟧” The Urantia Book says that this shows that even a young person, if the desire of the heart is true, can become a loving companion of the God of a universe.
p177.005: Jesus told John not to be discouraged by what was coming, and encouraged him that he would live on and become a strong messenger of the kingdom. On the way back, Jesus told him not to tell anyone what they had talked about that day, and John kept that promise all his life. From then on, John Mark hardly ever left Jesus' side.
p177.007: That day Jesus talked a lot with John about his childhood. Jesus told John that because he had grown up with parents who truly loved each other, he would become a dependable person. John's parents had wisdom as well as love: though they were well off, they did not spoil their son or raise him in luxury, and they let him learn about the world through his own experience. In contrast, the parents of John's friend Amos loved their son so much that they would not let him follow Jesus. Jesus urged him, “⟦Q 177:2.3⟧make sure that your love is admonished by wisdom and guided by intelligence.⟦/Q⟧”
p177.008: Jesus explained that a child learns all his first ideas, even his ideas of people and of God, at home. A child gets his first impression of the universe through his mother's care, and his first idea of the Father in heaven from his earthly father. The Urantia Book says that for Jesus' gospel, which is based on the relationship between a father and his children, to be widely accepted, homes need more love and wisdom. Families today have more freedom, it says, but that freedom is often not guided by love, loyalty, and wisdom. A good home makes religion strong, and true religion makes the home shine.
p177.010: All day long the apostles felt the Master's absence deeply and were worried. Every one of them except Judas secretly wished he were in John Mark's place. Nathaniel said, “⟦Q 177:3.2⟧What is wrong with most of us is that we are only halfhearted⟦/Q⟧”, and that if they had wanted it as badly as the boy, the Master would have taken them along too.
p177.011: In the afternoon word came to David Zebedee. David was sure that the rulers would kill Jesus and that Jesus would not defend himself, so he had already sent for Jesus' mother Mary and the family to come to Jerusalem, and they were on their way. David told no one about this. Also, more than twenty Greeks came and talked with Peter and John, and Jesus would have ordained them like the seventy if the apostles had not been so unsettled. In Jerusalem, the leaders wondered why Jesus had not come to the temple, and along with their Passover preparations they were finishing their plans to do away with him.
p177.013: Right after Jesus left, Judas Iscariot secretly went to Jerusalem and met with members of the Sanhedrin gathered at the house of the high priest Caiaphas. The day before, Judas had confided to his relatives that Jesus was only a well-meaning dreamer and not the deliverer of Israel, and his relatives urged him on, saying that if he left he would receive great honor from the rulers. Judas was sure that Jesus would not use his power to save himself and would end in failure, and he could not stand the humiliation of being part of a failed movement. On top of that, his jealousy and desire for revenge grew because only Peter, James, and John were close to Jesus. The Urantia Book says clearly that Judas did not betray Jesus for money.
p177.014: Introduced by his cousin, Judas came before Caiaphas and asked, “⟦Q 177:4.7⟧what are you willing to give me for this service?⟦/Q⟧” He was so drunk with his own glory that he did not even notice the contempt on Caiaphas's face. Judas consulted with the captain of the temple guards and agreed to have Jesus seized on Thursday night, when everyone was asleep.
p177.015: The Urantia Book explains that Judas had been storing up disappointment and resentment in his heart for a long time. He was bitter that Jesus had not saved John the Baptist when he was killed, and he was hurt every time Jesus turned down power and glory. Jesus loved and trusted Judas just as he did the other apostles, but Judas did not open his heart to that love. The other apostles had also once wanted worldly honors, but in their hearts they loved Jesus and the truth. The heavy lesson of this story is that even a love that was once sincere can turn into hatred if disappointment, jealousy, and resentment are held onto for a long time.
p177.017: In the evening there was a social hour, but the apostles could hardly cheer up. Jesus asked about each apostle's family one by one, and David Zebedee could not answer but only looked down at his feet. Jesus warned them not to be fooled by the great crowds at the temple who seemed to believe his teaching. Those who know the gospel only in the mind and have not experienced it in the heart scatter when trouble comes. And he urged them, “⟦Q 177:5.2⟧Watch, therefore, and pray⟦/Q⟧”.
p177.018: This Wednesday evening was the time when the apostles' hearts sank lowest. Around midnight, though he knew this was the last night he would sleep with his chosen family, Jesus wished them peace, saying that tomorrow would be another day to enjoy doing the Father's will. A heart that sincerely longs to be with Jesus, like John Mark's, and a home full of wise love help us grow into people who are not easily shaken.
p178.002: Thursday was the last free day that Jesus spent on earth in the flesh. Jesus decided to spend this day with his apostles and a few loyal disciples. After breakfast Jesus led them to a quiet place above the camp and taught them many new truths; this was his farewell discourse to the whole company of the camp. Only Judas was missing, and some of the apostles thought he had gone into the city to prepare for the Passover.
p178.004: For almost two hours, Jesus spoke to about fifty followers about the relation between the kingdom of heaven and the kingdoms of this world, and between being a son of God and being a citizen of a nation. Earthly governments sometimes use force to keep order, but the kingdom of heaven must be spread only by the power of the spirit. There is no conflict between being a son of God and being a good citizen. Believers are to “⟦Q 178:1.3⟧render to Caesar the things which are Caesar's and to God the things which are God's.⟦/Q⟧” But if a ruler demands to be worshiped as God, they must worship God alone. Nor should they borrow the power of government to spread the spiritual kingdom.
p178.005: Jesus said that becoming a son of the kingdom should make a person an even better citizen. Believers carry duties to people and duties to God, and also the duty of serving their brothers. Loving service is the lever that lifts the world, and the Spirit of Truth is its fulcrum. Truth must not be forced by law or power but must be spread by persuasion, and he told them never to forget the rule “⟦Q 178:1.12⟧Whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do even so to them.⟦/Q⟧” If rulers acted like religious tyrants, believers would be persecuted, but he said that the way they endured that suffering would in the end awaken the world, so that government and religion would be separated and all nations would enjoy freedom of faith. He also warned that a time more dangerous than persecution is a comfortable time when everyone praises believers, so they must stay faithful even in peaceful times. The many good works that help people are precious, he said, but none of them must ever take the place of preaching the gospel.
p178.006: Jesus said that believers should not become mystics or dreamers who withdraw from the world, but should be gentle and patient, and yet brave in proclaiming the truth. The gospel is like a living seed; it must grow in a new form in every generation and show ever greater power, and it must never become a mere old memory or tradition. He told them not to attack the old ways but to wisely put in the leaven of new truth. Finally he urged them to love one another, not to quarrel even with unbelievers, and to be loyal citizens, good neighbors, and understanding parents.
p178.008: Many people did not fully understand this discourse. The Greeks understood it best, and the apostles did not know how to fit his talk of the distant future together with their Master's coming departure. Some Jewish believers sensed that a great tragedy was coming, but seeing the Master's cheerful, calm manner, they grew even more confused. Around noon word went around that Lazarus had hurriedly fled from Bethany. David Zebedee even knew that Judas had joined the plot, but when he tried to ask Jesus about it, Jesus said that he knew everything, that David should tell no one, and that he should trust that God's will would be done. To Abner at Philadelphia he sent word to go on with his work, along with the words “⟦Q 178:2.4⟧I will not forsake you.⟦/Q⟧”
p178.009: When Philip asked where they should prepare the Passover meal, Jesus called Peter, John, and Philip aside and told them to follow a man carrying a water pitcher at the gate of Jerusalem. That man led them to the home of John Mark, where an upper room was ready for the supper. Jesus had arranged this with John Mark the day before, so that Judas would not know the place ahead of time and could not interrupt the last meal. Meanwhile, Judas handed over all the apostles' funds to David. About half past four in the afternoon, Jesus set out on his last journey with all twelve apostles.
p178.010: 3. On the Way to the Supper
p178.011: When they reached a spot on the Mount of Olives overlooking the city, Jesus rested until sunset and talked with the apostles one last time. Jesus said that he must soon leave, and that just as the Father had sent him, he was now sending them into the world to finish the work he had begun. He urged them not to throw themselves into danger needlessly when he was arrested, but to survive as witnesses of the gospel. They must be brave in defending the gospel, but they must not foolishly rush forward to defend the Son of Man.
p178.012: Jesus told them that even if they saw this city destroyed, they must not forget that they had already entered the eternal life of the kingdom of heaven, which goes on without end. There are many abodes in the Father's universe, and when they had finished their work on earth, they too would enter into the joy of their Lord. Then they walked into the city along the dim road. No one in the crowd knew that the Son of God was on his way to his last supper, and the apostles did not know that one of them had already planned a betrayal. John Mark ran ahead to his house to welcome them. Jesus' last teaching, to live as good citizens and as children of God, tells us that faith must show itself in honest everyday living and in love for our neighbors.
p179.002: When Philip asked about preparing for the Passover, he was thinking of the Passover supper to be eaten the next evening, Friday. So the apostles did not really understand why Jesus wanted to hold the supper a day early. Some apostles thought it was because Jesus knew he would be arrested before the Passover, while others thought it was a special gathering. Jesus had never taken part in the sacrifice of the lamb, so they did not think it strange that there was no lamb at this supper. Only the twelve apostles were to be at this supper, so there was no servant to wait on them.
p179.004: As they entered the upper room, the apostles saw the water pitchers, basins, and towels for washing feet beside the door. Since there was no servant, someone had to wash the feet, but each one secretly thought that it would not be he. At the table there was the host's seat and the seats of honor on either side of it. Then Judas stepped forward to take the seat of honor at the host's left, and right after that John took the place on the right. Angry, Peter went and sat in the lowest place, hoping that Jesus would come and call him up to a higher seat.
p179.005: Even at their last supper with Jesus, the apostles quarreled over honor and high places. While they were trading accusations, Jesus appeared at the door, and a look of disappointment came over his face. Without a word, Jesus went to his place and sat down.
p179.007: Jesus looked around at them all for a moment, then smiled and said, “⟦Q 179:2.1⟧I have greatly desired to eat this Passover with you.⟦/Q⟧” Then he gave thanks over the cup of wine and had them share it, saying that he would not drink with them like this again until they sat together once more in the kingdom to come.
p179.008: Jesus knew that his hour had come and that he had almost finished the purpose for which he had come into this world. He also knew that Judas meant to hand him over to his enemies that night. But Jesus was not afraid of those who wanted to kill his body, nor of the forces that wanted to destroy him spiritually. His only concern was the safety and salvation of his beloved disciples. So now he set out to act out a parable that would show brotherly love.
p179.010: After the first cup, Jesus quietly rose, took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist, and poured water into a basin. Then he went to Peter, who was sitting in the lowest place, and knelt like a servant. All twelve apostles jumped to their feet in astonishment. Peter refused—“⟦Q 179:3.3⟧Master, you shall never wash my feet!⟦/Q⟧”—but when Jesus said that unless he washed his feet Peter could have no part with him, Peter asked him to wash his hands and head too. In silence Jesus went around the table and washed the feet of all twelve, not leaving out Judas. Even seeing this humble act, Judas took it as proof that Jesus was not fit to be a deliverer.
p179.011: Back in his place, Jesus asked why, when their Master had washed their feet, they had been unwilling to wash one another's feet. And he said, “⟦Q 179:3.8⟧A servant is not greater than his master⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus said that at his table there were no better seats, and that he loved them all equally. The kings of the world rule over their people, but in the kingdom of heaven, whoever would be great must become like the younger, and whoever would be chief must become one who serves. Jesus said, “⟦Q 179:3.9⟧you will observe that I am among you as one who serves.⟦/Q⟧”
p179.013: As the meal went on, Jesus said that he must soon go to the Father, but that it had not been necessary for one of them to hand him over to his enemies. Upset, the apostles each asked, “⟦Q 179:4.2⟧Is it I?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said that this was the fruit of the evil hidden in the heart of one who had failed to love the truth with his whole soul, and that an old friend who was now dipping his hand in the dish with him would betray him. When Judas asked, “⟦Q 179:4.3⟧Is it I?⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus handed him a dipped piece of bread and said, “⟦Q 179:4.3⟧You have said⟦/Q⟧”, but the other apostles did not hear these words.
p179.014: Jesus said he was telling them about this sad thing ahead of time so that they would be strengthened for the trials to come. Then he said to Judas, “⟦Q 179:4.6⟧What you have decided to do, do quickly⟦/Q⟧”, and Judas went straight out into the night. The other apostles thought he had simply gone on an errand. Jesus tried to save Judas right up to the last moment, and his warm gestures at this supper were his last appeal to Judas. But The Urantia Book says that once love has died, even kind warnings may only make hatred grow.
p179.016: When he was handed the third cup, the “⟦Q 179:5.1⟧cup of blessing⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus rose and blessed it, saying that this would be the cup of his remembrance and a sign of the coming of the Spirit of Truth. The old Passover remembered how their fathers came out of slavery, but now Jesus established a supper to remember a new age, in which people are set free from the bondage of ceremony and selfishness and enter the brotherhood of the children of God. Then he broke the bread and shared it, saying, “⟦Q 179:5.3⟧I have told you that I am the bread of life.⟦/Q⟧”
p179.017: The Urantia Book explains that Jesus deliberately used parable and symbol so that later generations could not tie this supper down to rigid formulas or doctrines. He wanted to leave the spiritual imagination of believers free. Yet later this teaching became the most tradition-bound of all Jesus' teachings. The Urantia Book says that when believers take part in this supper, the Master is truly present with them. This took place with no sacred building and no ceremony, in the upper room of a friend's house.
p179.018: Jesus said, “⟦Q 179:5.9⟧And as often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me.⟦/Q⟧” He told them to remember the life he had lived with them and to believe that someday they would share a supper together in the Father's kingdom. And he urged them not to quarrel over who was greatest but to live together as brothers. They sang a psalm together and ended the supper. Like Jesus, who washed the feet of disciples who were fighting over the highest places, the person who first becomes humble and serves is the one who is truly great.
p180.002: After the Last Supper, the apostles expected to head straight back to camp, but Jesus asked them to sit down. He reminded them that before, he had sent them out without a purse or extra clothes, and they had lacked nothing. But now hard times had come, so when they went out to preach the gospel, they should make their own plans to support themselves. Then he said that in a little while he would go where they could not go now, but when they finished their work on earth, they would come to him.
p180.004: Jesus stood up and gave them a new commandment. The apostles already knew the commandment “⟦Q 180:1.1⟧that you love your neighbor even as yourself⟦/Q⟧”, but Jesus wanted an even greater love from them. This was the commandment “⟦Q 180:1.1⟧That you love one another even as I have loved you⟦/Q⟧”. If they loved one another like that, everyone would know they were his disciples. Jesus said this commandment was not a new burden but a new joy of sharing love.
p180.005: Jesus said there is no greater love than to lay down your life for your friends, and now he called them not servants but friends. The Urantia Book explains that what Jesus wants is not sacrifice but loyalty. Doing something out of forced duty is the attitude of a servant, but service a friend gives for a friend is a joy that cannot be called sacrifice. This kind of love does not remove the world's difficulties, but it makes the old world new.
p180.007: Jesus said, “⟦Q 180:2.1⟧I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus is the vine, and the apostles are the branches. Just as a branch dries up when it is cut off from the vine, we cannot bear the fruit of loving service unless we stay in Jesus. When the branches on the vine bear much fruit, the Father is glorified. Even when the farmer prunes the branches, it is a loving touch meant to help them bear more fruit.
p180.008: The Urantia Book explains that what Jesus said about prayer at this time was later misunderstood. People treated praying in Jesus' name like a kind of magic that gets you anything, and because of that many were disappointed and their faith was shaken. But prayer is not a way to get your own will done; it is an experience of learning to know and follow God's will. Just as whatever a living branch asks for, the answer is more fruit, believers live to bear the fruit of loving one another as Jesus has loved us.
p180.010: Jesus told them not to lose heart even if the world hated them. The world had hated Jesus first, and a servant is not greater than his master. They were in the world, but they must not live the way the world lives. Jesus promised he would not leave them alone; he would soon send a spirit helper. And he said, “⟦Q 180:3.4⟧Let not your hearts be troubled⟦/Q⟧”, telling them that there are many places to stay in the Father's universe, and that someday they too would rise up there and be with him.
p180.011: When Thomas said he did not know where the Master was going or the way there, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 180:3.7⟧I am the way, the truth, and the life⟦/Q⟧”. When Philip asked him to show them the Father, Jesus said, “⟦Q 180:3.9⟧He who has seen me has seen the Father⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus said the Father was in him and worked through him, so if they found it hard to believe his words, they should at least believe because of the life he had lived.
p180.013: Jesus promised that after he returned to the Father and received sovereignty over his universe, he would pour out the Spirit of Truth on all people. Right now he was with them only in his body, but from then on, by his spirit, he could be with everyone at the same time, wherever they were. That is why Jesus said his leaving was actually better. This spirit would comfort and guide them and would remind them of everything Jesus had taught.
p180.014: Judas the son of Alpheus asked how they could recognize the Master if he came only in spirit. Jesus smiled and said that soon he would send a spirit just like himself, only without a material body. This spirit would live in each person's heart and bind the children of light together as one, and in this way the Father and the Son would live in the hearts of all who love one another.
p180.016: The Urantia Book explains that the Spirit of Truth is not words on a page or a law, but a living conviction about truth. Truth can be known, lived, and grown in the heart, but if you lock it up in formulas or creeds, it soon dies. The Urantia Book says, “⟦Q 180:5.2⟧Static truth is dead truth⟦/Q⟧”. A person who knows God lifts wisdom up to the level of living truth.
p180.017: The Urantia Book gives the golden rule as an example. If you take 'do to others as you would have them do to you' only word for word, you might reason that since you want to hear honest words, you should tell others every thought you have, and so actually hurt them. The golden rule, understood spiritually, means treating the people you meet so that they receive the greatest good from you. The teaching about not resisting evil is the same: you can understand its meaning only when you live it, not as a rule but under the leading of the Spirit of Truth.
p180.018: The Urantia Book says that while the old religion taught self-sacrifice, the new gospel teaches us to find our true selves by forgetting ourselves in serving others. The old religion was driven by fear, but the new gospel is led by the Spirit of Truth. No show of piety or creed can make up for a lack of real compassion for our neighbors.
p180.020: Jesus warned that a time would come when those who killed them would think they were serving God. He told them this ahead of time so that, when that time came, they would remember that Jesus had known everything and that his spirit was with them, and they would find strength. Then, honestly, like a friend, he told them that his leaving was good for them. Only if he left could the Spirit of Truth come and guide them into all truth.
p180.021: When the apostles whispered among themselves, not knowing what “⟦Q 180:6.6⟧little while⟦/Q⟧” meant, Jesus told them that the Son of Man would die and then live again. Just as a woman in labor forgets her pain and rejoices once her child is born, their sorrow would soon turn to joy. He also said that because people cannot see the Father, who is spirit, he had come to show them the Father, but that when their spirits were fully grown, they would see the Father directly. But the apostles still could not let go of their old idea of a glorious kingdom on earth, and they still did not understand. The new commandment to love one another as Jesus has loved us can begin today, with the friends and family right beside us.
p181.002: After finishing the farewell discourse, Jesus talked with the apostles in a relaxed way. Only now were the apostles slowly beginning to realize that Jesus, their friend and teacher, was soon going away. But they took his promise to come back after a little while to mean that he would make a short visit to the Father and then soon set up the kingdom on earth. That interpretation fit perfectly with the beliefs and hopes they had held for so long. After a while, Jesus quieted them again and began to give his final admonitions and warnings.
p181.004: Jesus said that while he lived in the flesh, he could only be one person in one place, but once he laid aside this body, he could return as a spirit and live in every believer. He also said that eternal life in the Father's creation is not lazy rest but endless growth, and that the children of light go on from glory to glory. He urged them that, to follow him, they should not copy the outward details of the life he had lived, but follow the spirit and ideals of that life of doing the Father's will. Jesus said he would soon pour out the Spirit of Truth on all people, but not everyone would receive it. Yet for those who did, this spirit would become a spring of living water welling up to eternal life.
p181.005: Saying “⟦Q 181:1.5⟧my peace I give to you⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus left them a peace different from what the world gives. The apostles would be scattered by persecution and feel lonely, but Jesus told them to take courage, saying, “⟦Q 181:1.5⟧I have overcome the world⟦/Q⟧”. He said that he himself would soon be left alone, yet he was never really alone, because the Father was always with him. The Urantia Book explains that a person without faith has only two kinds of peace to lean on: the peace of the stoic, who grits his teeth and endures what cannot be avoided, and the peace of the optimist, who vaguely hopes for good days that will never come. Jesus was neither. Jesus' peace was the peace of a son who trusted that his life was completely safe in the hands of a wise and loving Father. That is why, even though he knew everything that lay ahead, Jesus could say, “⟦Q 181:1.9⟧Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid⟦/Q⟧”.
p181.007: Jesus went around the table and gave each apostle a personal farewell and admonition. To John, the youngest, he entrusted the care of his family and told him to become the apostle of the new commandment and spend his life teaching people how to love one another. When John asked how he could love his brothers more, Jesus answered that he should first love the Father in heaven more and truly care about his brothers' welfare. Jesus paused sadly for a moment beside the empty seat of Judas, but the apostles did not notice what it meant. To Simon Zelotes, the patriot, he said that Simon would be deeply discouraged when he failed to realize that the kingdom is not of this world, but that even then the Master would be with him and he would always be an apostle. Jesus told Simon to think deeply about the teaching to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's, and to show how to be a good citizen and also a son of the heavenly kingdom. And he reminded him again that those who fight with the sword perish by the sword, but those who work by the spirit enjoy joy and peace.
p181.008: To Matthew, the former tax collector, he said to spend his life showing that God is no respecter of persons and that every believer is a son of God. Jesus told him that he knew all about how Matthew had quietly worked to keep the apostles' treasury supplied, and that all the apostles loved him. To James, who had once sought a high position, he said that soon he would have the experience of drinking the Master's cup. He told him to keep his soul by patience, to learn caution along with courage, and to live as long as he could to bear the fruit of the gospel. Andrew, who had led the apostles, was now released from his duties of administration, but Jesus asked him to hold his brothers together in love during the time of trial ahead. Jesus explained that wherever two or more people work together, there must always be orderly leadership. He added that even if Andrew did not do great things himself, he should be content to be an adviser to those who do. To the Alpheus twins he said that even if they went back to their old work, they should show that for a person who knows God there is no such thing as common labor; all work is holy.
p181.009: To Philip, who was always saying 'show us,' he said to lead people now to seek God with the spiritual eyes of faith. To honest Nathaniel he said that sincerity is most useful when it is paired with discretion. When Nathaniel confessed that he was confused because he did not fully understand the gospel, Jesus told him that the best teachers, real experience and the Spirit of Truth, would teach him in the future. To doubting Thomas he said that he had shown courage even when he doubted, and told him to show that a life bearing the fruits of love overcomes doubt. Finally, he urged Peter to think before he spoke. When Peter said he would follow the Master even to death, Jesus told him that before the cock crowed that night he would deny him, but that after he had learned this painful lesson, he should strengthen his brothers. And to all the apostles he said that, just as the sheep scatter when the shepherd is struck, they were all in danger of stumbling that night, but he promised that he would come back for a little while and go ahead of them into Galilee. Jesus told them he loved them with the same love with which the Father loved him, and after singing a hymn, they left for the camp on the Mount of Olives. Jesus loved and believed in each of his imperfect followers just as they were. Each of us, too, has a place entrusted to us within that kind of love.
p182.002: Around ten o'clock on Thursday night, Jesus left the home of John Mark with the eleven apostles and headed for the Gethsemane camp. John Mark, who had dozed off for a moment, heard them coming down, threw on a linen coat, and followed them. From then on, he watched everything up close, right through to the cross. On the way back, the apostles began for the first time to suspect Judas. When Judas was not at the camp, they all asked Andrew about it, and Andrew only answered, “⟦Q 182:0.2⟧I fear he has deserted us⟦/Q⟧”.
p182.004: Jesus led the apostles up to a flat rock on the Mount of Olives and had them kneel in a circle around him, just as on the day of their ordination. Then, in the moonlight, he lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed. Jesus said that eternal life is to know the Father as the only true God and to believe in the one he sent. He also said that he had finished the work the Father gave him, and now all that was left was to lay down his life in the flesh. Jesus did not ask the Father to take the apostles out of the world, but to keep them from the evil in the world and make them holy in the truth. And for all who would believe in the future, he prayed that they would all be one, just as the Father and the Son are one.
p182.005: The Urantia Book explains that although Jesus prayed for his followers to be one, he did not want them all to be the same. In a living fellowship with God, there can be no final word on doctrine and no one denomination that is better than the rest. Jesus also said in his prayer that he had shown the Father's name to the world. To Moses, God had been made known only as “⟦Q 182:1.9⟧I AM⟦/Q⟧”, but Jesus revealed the Father with his whole life, so he could say, “⟦Q 182:1.10⟧I am the bread of life⟦/Q⟧”, “⟦Q 182:1.16⟧I am the good shepherd⟦/Q⟧”, and “⟦Q 182:1.20⟧I am the way, the truth, and the life⟦/Q⟧”.
p182.007: When they got back to camp, the apostles were deeply shocked to learn that Judas was the betrayer. When David Zebedee and John Mark reported that they had been keeping an eye on Judas, Jesus told them not to worry, because nothing would happen to the Son of Man unless the Father in heaven willed it. Jesus' usual cheerful manner was slowly turning serious and sorrowful. With the words “⟦Q 182:2.2⟧My peace I leave with you⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus told the apostles to go and rest, and he asked only Peter, James, and John to stay. Simon Zelotes handed out swords to the apostles, but Nathaniel refused, saying the Master's kingdom is not set up by the sword: “⟦Q 182:2.3⟧I will pray, but I will not wield the sword⟦/Q⟧”. Andrew gave his sword back, too.
p182.008: Jesus sent a messenger to Abner in Philadelphia to tell him that he would be killed but would rise again and appear to him. He told the Greeks who were with them the same thing, and he asked Andrew to keep his brothers together until he came again. The apostles went to sleep, thinking nothing would happen that night. As David Zebedee went off to guard the road, he told Jesus that he had sent for Jesus' family and that they would arrive the next morning. To David, who had wholeheartedly done small jobs like running messages, Jesus said, “⟦Q 182:2.10⟧You, too, shall some day serve with me in the eternal kingdom⟦/Q⟧”. John Mark finally left his post, followed Jesus, hid in the bushes, and watched everything.
p182.010: Jesus took Peter, James, and John to the ravine where he usually prayed. The three apostles had never seen their Master so weighed down by sorrow. Jesus told them to stay awake, and a little distance away he prayed with his face to the ground. But when he came back, he found his followers worn out and asleep. Jesus asked, “⟦Q 182:3.2⟧can you not watch with me even for one hour?⟦/Q⟧” During his second prayer, a mighty angel came down and strengthened him. The third time, Jesus prayed, “⟦Q 182:3.4⟧Not my will, but yours, be done⟦/Q⟧”, and, looking at his sleeping followers, he asked the Father to have mercy on them, saying, “⟦Q 182:3.4⟧The spirit is indeed willing, but the flesh is weak⟦/Q⟧”. When he had finished praying, Jesus woke them and said that the time of decision was past and the one who would betray him was near.
p182.011: The Urantia Book explains that through these prayers, Jesus' human will became more and more one with the Father's will. The angel brought word that the Father wished the Son to finish his life on earth by experiencing death, as all people do. Jesus was tired from his long labors, and it hurt him deeply to leave his weak apostles behind. He was away from his family, and he was being betrayed by a close companion. In anguish so deep that his sweat fell in great drops, Jesus made up his mind completely not to use his power as ruler of the universe to save himself. Countless heavenly beings were watching, but they had been told not to step in unless Jesus commanded it.
p182.012: In the middle of this great sorrow, Jesus steadied his heart by remembering his childhood in Nazareth and the beautiful sunrises and sunsets over the Sea of Galilee. And before Judas and the soldiers arrived, he had fully regained his calm. The spirit had won over the flesh, and faith had won over fear and doubt. Jesus, who even in his hardest moment prayed to do as the Father willed, shows us that when we are afraid and lonely, we too can find the strength to stand up again if we trust our hearts to God.
p183.002: Jesus woke Peter, James, and John and told them to go to their tents and sleep, but they were already wide awake. Urgent messengers came looking for David Zebedee, and the Greeks camped nearby came out armed, so the whole camp was stirring. Jesus would not let anyone wake the eight sleeping apostles. Then, so that those coming to arrest him would take only him and leave the apostles alone, he went by himself to the olive press at the entrance to the Gethsemane park and sat down. He was worried that if the apostles saw Judas's betrayal, they would get excited, fight back, and be caught and killed along with him. The only ones who watched this were John Mark, hiding in a shed, and countless heavenly observers.
p183.004: The Urantia Book stresses that we should not misunderstand what happened in Jesus' last hours. It was not the will of the Father in heaven that Jesus be treated cruelly by servants and soldiers or be given an unfair trial. The Father's will was for the Son to fully experience human life, from birth to death, as all people do. Just as ordinary people cannot escape the last moments of life by some special help, Jesus chose to lay down his life by the natural course of events, and he refused to save himself.
p183.005: But the hatred and cruelty that came out along the way were the doings of wicked men. The Urantia Book says that the God of heaven did not want this, and that even the father of sin turned his face away from the terrible scene of the cross. What Jesus promised in Gethsemane was to trust himself to the Father to the very end; the people's violence itself was not God's plan.
p183.007: After slipping away from the supper, Judas went with his cousin to the captain of the temple guards and gathered the guards. But when they reached the home of John Mark, Jesus and the apostles had already left fifteen minutes earlier. Judas was badly flustered. He knew there were more than sixty disciples at the camp and that Simon Zelotes had weapons. On top of that, when he thought about how much the apostles would hate him, he grew more and more afraid. The Urantia Book says that he was not only disloyal but at heart a coward.
p183.008: Judas demanded forty armed soldiers to protect himself. The Jewish leaders told him Jesus had always taught nonresistance, but Judas was not reassured. Using Roman soldiers required permission, so for more than an hour they went from one official to another, until finally they went all the way to the governor, Pilate. Pilate granted the request of the head of the Sanhedrin, even though his wife urged him not to. And so, at about half past eleven at night, a crowd of more than sixty, including guards, Roman soldiers, and servants, set out behind Judas.
p183.010: As the crowd with torches came near, Judas went out in front so that he would not look like he was with the soldiers, but Jesus greeted him kindly, yet as a betrayer. To keep Judas from betraying him even at the last moment, Jesus spoke first, before Judas could reach him, asking the Roman captain, “⟦Q 183:3.4⟧Whom do you seek?⟦/Q⟧” At the answer, “⟦Q 183:3.4⟧Jesus of Nazareth⟦/Q⟧”, Jesus said with majesty, “⟦Q 183:3.4⟧I am he⟦/Q⟧”, and the men in front fell backward in surprise. Now there was no need for Judas to step forward, but to earn the promised reward and honor, he went up to Jesus and kissed him on the forehead. Jesus said, “⟦Q 183:3.5⟧Would you even betray the Son of Man with a kiss?⟦/Q⟧”
p183.011: Jesus told them to take him but to let the others go. But when Malchus, the high priest's servant, moved to bind Jesus' hands, Peter drew his sword and rushed at him. Jesus stopped him at once, saying, “⟦Q 183:3.7⟧Peter, put up your sword. They who take the sword shall perish by the sword⟦/Q⟧”, and he said that he could have the help of countless angels if he wished, but that he would drink this cup according to the Father's will. The guards tied Jesus with ropes, and Jesus asked why they had come with swords and clubs as if to catch a robber, when they had not seized him while he taught openly in the temple every day.
p183.012: When the captain of the guards ordered them to seize the followers as well, everyone fled into the ravine. John Mark, who had been hiding in the shed, was grabbed by the edge of his coat by a soldier as he slipped out, but he threw off the coat, escaped, and told David. Peter and John Zebedee followed behind as Jesus was led away, John close by and Peter far behind.
p183.014: The remaining apostles and disciples gathered by the olive press to decide what to do. Andrew, who had now stepped down from leadership, was silent. Simon Zelotes climbed up on the stone wall and shouted that they should go after Jesus and rescue him, but Nathaniel reminded them that the Master had taught nonresistance and had told them to save their lives so they could preach the gospel. James told them how Jesus had ordered Peter to put away his sword, and Thomas persuaded them to scatter, saying that since the Master had refused to defend himself, they could not save him.
p183.015: By about half past two in the morning, the camp was empty. Five apostles hid in Bethpage and Bethany, and four hid in the city. David Zebedee stayed at the camp and, through his messengers, sent news to the scattered followers and to Jesus' family. Near dawn, Peter came back in deep despair. The Urantia Book says, “⟦Q 183:4.6⟧Surely, the shepherd is smitten and the sheep are scattered!⟦/Q⟧” They dimly understood that Jesus had warned them ahead of time, but they were too shocked to think clearly. When day broke, Jesus' brother Jude arrived, but he only heard that Jesus had already been arrested, and the family waited for news in Bethany.
p183.016: 5. On the Way to the High Priest’s Palace
p183.017: By order of the Roman captain, Jesus was first taken to the house of Annas, the former high priest. The two captains despised Judas so much that they would not say a word to him. When John Zebedee came up beside Jesus, the captain of the temple guards ordered him to be bound, but the Roman captain said, “⟦Q 183:5.3⟧This man is neither a traitor nor a coward⟦/Q⟧”, and ordered that no one touch this man, who had not drawn a sword but had bravely stood by his Master. When Judas heard this, he was so ashamed that he dropped back behind the crowd.
p183.018: The Roman captain told his aide to see to it that the Jewish leaders did not put Jesus to death without Pilate's permission, and to let his friend stay at his side and see everything. That is why, while the other apostles had to stay in hiding, John was able to be with Jesus all the way to the cross. All the way to the palace of Annas, Jesus did not say a single word. Like John, who overcame his fear and stayed by Jesus to the end when everyone else scattered, standing by someone in hard times is true love and courage.
p184.002: When Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane, the soldiers took him straight to the palace of Annas, the former high priest. Annas was the most powerful religious leader in Jewish society, and he wanted to hold Jesus for a few hours to gain time to gather the Sanhedrin (the highest Jewish religious court). Meanwhile, about thirty members of the Sanhedrin who opposed Jesus had gathered at the home of Caiaphas, the high priest and Annas's son-in-law, to wait for the trial. Because John Zebedee was a distant relative of Annas's family, he was able to stay by Jesus' side inside the palace.
p184.004: Annas had come to hate Jesus bitterly after Jesus drove the money-changers out of the temple and threatened his income. He thought he might persuade Jesus to leave Palestine, but when he stood before the dignified and calm Jesus, he soon realized that such an offer was useless. When asked for the names of his followers, Jesus did not answer.
p184.005: When Annas boasted of his power, Jesus said that he could have no power at all unless the Father allowed it, and then he kindly asked him a question instead: knowing what he knew, how could he reject the light of God? When asked about his teaching, Jesus said that he had always taught openly, so Annas should ask those who had heard him. At that, the steward struck Jesus in the face. Jesus quietly asked, “⟦Q 184:1.6⟧if I have spoken the truth, why, then, should you smite me?⟦/Q⟧” When Annas asked whether he claimed to be the Messiah, Jesus answered that he had been sent not only to the Jews but to all people. In the end, Annas had Jesus bound and sent him to Caiaphas.
p184.007: In the meantime, thanks to John, Simon Peter had come into the courtyard of Annas and was warming himself by the charcoal fire. In fact, he should not have been there, because Jesus had warned the apostles not to put their lives in danger. When the woman at the gate and the servants asked him again and again, “⟦Q 184:2.4⟧Are you not also one of this man's disciples?⟦/Q⟧” Peter, terrified, denied several times that he knew Jesus.
p184.008: When he denied him the last time, the cock crowed, and Peter remembered Jesus' warning. Just then Jesus, being led away to Caiaphas, turned and looked at him, with a look of mingled pity and love. Peter sat down by the roadside and wept bitterly. The Urantia Book says that once we start down a wrong path, it is easy to keep justifying that choice, and it takes great character to turn back to the right way. Only after meeting Jesus after the resurrection did Peter fully believe he had been forgiven.
p184.010: At half past three on Friday morning, Caiaphas opened a special court of Sanhedrin members in his palace. This was not a regular meeting, and Caiaphas acted more like a prosecutor than a fair judge. More than twenty false witnesses came forward, but their stories did not agree with one another, so much so that even the members were embarrassed. Jesus kept silent with a gentle face, and that calm silence became the best answer to the false charges. Annas seized on Jesus' saying that he would destroy the temple and raise it again in three days, trying to paint him as a dangerous man who deceived the people and meant to harm the temple.
p184.011: When Caiaphas could stand it no longer and demanded, in the name of the living God, whether he was the Son of God, Jesus answered clearly, “⟦Q 184:3.14⟧I am⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus paid no attention to the other questions, but he answered at once the one question about his bestowal mission (his mission of coming to this earth as a man, as the Son of God). Caiaphas tore his clothes and cried out that it was blasphemy, and everyone shouted that he should be crucified. The Urantia Book says that people blinded by prejudice tried to judge the Creator of the universe, yet even then he loved them.
p184.013: According to Jewish law, a death sentence required a second session of the court on the following day, but they waited only one hour. During that hour, the guards and servants mocked Jesus, spat on him, beat him, and taunted him, “⟦Q 184:4.1⟧Prophesy to us, you the Deliverer, who it was that struck you⟦/Q⟧”. Jesus sent John into the next room so that he would not lose his life in anger, and Jesus himself said not a word.
p184.014: The Urantia Book says that this hour was the bitterest part of the cup of humiliation Jesus drank, yet at the same time it was the moment of his greatest triumph. Jesus did not defend himself, but he was not defenseless, and he was not defeated. Jesus, who had shown God to people, was now showing people to God. The Urantia Book explains that whoever experiences the religion of Jesus is set free from the fear of loneliness and isolation and becomes one within the family of God.
p184.015: 5. The Second Meeting of the Court
p184.016: The court met again at half past five and drew up the charges to bring to Pilate, the Roman governor. Annas believed that Pilate would not care about religious matters such as blasphemy. So they wrote down three charges: that Jesus misled the people and stirred up rebellion, that he taught people not to pay taxes to Caesar, and that he claimed to be a king.
p184.017: This whole process was against Jewish law as well. The witnesses' stories did not agree, no one spoke in Jesus' defense, and the charges were decided when Jesus was not even present. Seeing this, three Pharisees left. At six in the morning, Jesus was led before Pilate. The way Jesus never lost his calm and his love, even in the middle of lies and uproar, makes us think about what kind of heart we should keep when we are treated unfairly.
